newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-BOLDON'S TALENT CATCHING UP WITH HIS EGO.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-BOLDON'S TALENT CATCHING UP WITH HIS EGO.

text.p: Ato Boldon, the uninhibited Trinidadian sprinter, believes his talent is starting to catch up with his ego.
Talking to reporters on Friday on the eve of the sixth world championships, Boldon forecast Donovan Bailey's world record of 9.84 seconds would fall this weekend.
"I predicted a world record in Atlanta last year, and I was right. I was just wrong about who did it," he said.
Boldon, 23, won bronze in both the 100 and 200 at the Atlanta Olympics and is competing in both events here.
"The track is about the same at Atlanta. I think you are going to have 9.7 or 9.8, which is what I am predicting," he said.
"If my talents catch up with my ego, I would run 9.69 and 19.00 (for the 200)," Boldon said to a roar of laughter.,
Taking a day off from the track to rest sore shins, Boldon said Bailey remained the man to beat in the 100 metres.

"Every sprinter that has come to this meet wants what Donovan Bailey has," Boldon said of the world and Olympic champion and world record holder. "He's going to be here and he's going to be ready. If he wasn't ready, he wouldn't be here."
As for the 200 metres, Boldon said he would some day destroy Michael Johnson's world record of 19.32 seconds.
"I want to send my grandchildren to college on the money I'm going to make from breaking that record," Boldon said.

"I think within the next four years I should be able to challenge that record. If I didn't think realistically that I could break that record, I would stop because certainly the 100 can pay the bills."

Boldon, who trains with American champion Maurice Greene, clocked 9.90 seconds for the 100 and 19.77 for the 200 -- the fastest one-day double ever - at Stuttgart last month and earlier in the season ran 9.89, the year's fastest time.
"I think it is about time the history of the sport went in the past, and the future be the present," he said. "And we want to be the present."
Boldon concluded by praising nine times Olympic gold medallist Carl Lewis and double Olympic silver medallist Frank Fredericks for their willingness to run both the 100 and 200 metres.
"When I want to look at perfection, I look at Carl," he said.
